newsitem.title: USA: US Prudential tells court of more destroyed files.
newsitem.headline: US Prudential tells court of more destroyed files.

text.p: Prudential Insurance Co of America told the judge overseeing its massive class-action case that it has uncovered another incident of document destruction, this time at a sales office in Iowa.

In a December 27 letter to U.S. district judge Alfred Wolin, Prudential said about 150 documents were apparently removed and discarded from roughly 200 files in a Des Moines office. However, Prudential said it does not believe any actual sales documentation was discarded.
This incident follows at least two other similar situations earlier this year, one in Massachusetts and the other in Florida.
The documents are at issue because they could be relevant to the settlement of a class action against Prudential for improper sales practices.
Prudential said it continues to investigate the facts surrounding these events and is seriously concerned that some employees failed to observe its document retention policy.
The employees involved in the matter are currently under a disciplinary review, Prudential said.
Earlier this month, Prudential said it discovered the destruction of documents at a Cambridge, Massachusetts office.
A court-ordered investigation into that incident was completed late last week and a report on the matter is expected to be made public early next week.
Prudential has dismissed the managing director of the Cambridge office.
In August, Prudential fired a senior vice president after a company investigation found that files from a Jacksonville, Fla., office were discarded in a reorganization and relocation of staff.
In a related matter, Prudential said it has requested an administrative hearing to respond to charges in Florida that it blocked the state's probe into its life insurance sales practices.

The Florida insurance department and attorney general's office earlier this month filed a formal administrative complaint alleging the company obstructed their investigation, destroyed documents and ignored subpoenas.
A hearing date will be scheduled within the next two weeks, the Florida insurance department said.
In its request for a hearing, Prudential said Florida's administrative complaint contains sweeping generalizations, inaccuracies and mischaracterizations.
